name: Declinism
statement: People report that other people are getting less kind and honest, while survey measures of how their contemporaries behave stay flat across the same decades.
meaning: Declinism is a belief about the world, not a memory of one's own life. The version that has been tested is narrow. Asked whether people in general have become less honest, kind or trustworthy, respondents say yes, in every decade and nearly every country where the question has been put. The case for calling that an illusion rests on a mismatch between two kinds of survey question. Items that ask people to compare now with then produce reports of decline. Items that ask people to report the behaviour they met in the past year produce flat lines. Neither kind of item measures morality directly, and no objective register of everyday kindness exists to check either against. The unit of the finding is the survey item and the population average, not the individual respondent.

origin.who: Richard P. Eibach, Lisa K. Libby and Thomas D. Gilovich
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper "When change in the self is mistaken for change in the world" opened with two American surveys from 2000, each pairing a personal change with a judgement about society. In the General Social Survey, how a respondent's own finances had moved went with what they said had happened to freedom in America. In the National Election Study, people who had become parents since 1992 were likelier to say crime had risen, 38% of them against 29% of the rest, at a time when recorded crime had fallen. The authors proposed that misattributing self-change to world-change helps explain widespread beliefs in societal decline. The word "declinism" is older than the psychology. No academic source for its coinage was found in OpenAlex or Europe PMC on 21 September 2026, and the Oxford English Dictionary entry for the word is behind a subscription, so no date of first use is given here. Feng, Wildschut, Sedikides and Dang take their 2025 definition from the Cambridge Dictionary, a belief that everything is gradually becoming less, worse or lower, and add a gloss of their own, that core elements of society have deteriorated as time has passed.

evidence: Mastroianni and Gilbert assembled the survey record in 2023. They searched the Roper iPoll database and the archives of the General Social Survey, Pew, Gallup, the American National Election Studies, the World Values Survey and the European Social and Values Surveys. That turned up 177 items putting the question to 220,772 representative US respondents between 1949 and 2019. On 84.18% of those items a majority reported that morality had declined. The year of the survey did not predict that proportion, b = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.24], t(175) = 0.77, P = 0.45, with a Bayes factor of 0.04 against an effect. A second sweep found 58 items covering 354,120 people in 59 other nations between 1996 and 2007, and a majority reported decline on 86.21% of them. Respondents were not uniformly gloomy: 59% reported improved treatment of African Americans, 51% for people with physical disabilities and 50% for gay people. Their study 4 turned to items about present conduct, such as whether the respondent had been treated with respect yesterday or had let a stranger go ahead in a queue. Across 107 items put to 4,483,136 Americans between 1965 and 2020, the survey year explained under 0.3% of the variance on average, and under 0.2% across 33 non-US samples totalling 7,432,736 people. The whole paper covers 12,492,983 people. In their own study 2a, 698 Prolific respondents rated people as less kind, honest, nice and good in 2020 (M = 4.39) than in 2000 (M = 4.91), d = -0.71. Two mechanisms are proposed together as BEAM, biased exposure and biased memory: attention and media skew towards bad news about strangers, and negative memories fade faster, so the present looks worse than a past that has been quietly cleaned up. Two predictions followed. In study 5a, 283 respondents said people in general had declined between 2005 and 2020 (M = -0.36, d = 0.36) but that the individuals in their own personal world had improved (M = 0.23, t(255) = 4.86, d = 0.30). In study 5b, 387 respondents perceived decline after their own birth but none before it: ratings for the birth year and for 20 years earlier were equivalent (100% of the high-density interval inside the region of practical equivalence). Protzko and Schooler had already found the same shape in beliefs about the young. Their paper runs five preregistered studies, and the 3,458 American adults it reports in the abstract are the three studies covering traits, not the whole set. Respondents said children respect their elders less than they used to (b = 0.503, SE = 0.112, P < 0.001, n = 1,824) and enjoy reading less (b = 1.189, SE = 0.114, P < 0.001, n = 1,500). Which decline a person perceived tracked what that person was good at. Authoritarian respondents saw less respect, well-read respondents saw less reading, and more intelligent respondents saw falling intelligence. The crime version is visible in Gallup's own numbers. Frank Newport reports that in all but three of 32 measures taken since 1989, majorities of Americans have said crime nationally is increasing, which does not fit the recorded crime data. In the poll of 1 to 16 October 2025, 49% said there was more crime in the United States than a year earlier, against 30% who said so of their own area. On seriousness the gap was wider: 49% called national crime extremely or very serious against 12% for local crime.

examples.tag: The neighbourhood that used to look after itself
examples.text: A man tells his son that people once helped each other and now nobody bothers, then lists the neighbours who took the bins in and fed the cat while he was away. The verdict on his era does not move when the cases in front of him contradict it.

examples.tag: The staff room verdict on this year's intake
examples.text: Teachers agree that pupils have lost their manners since they started, while the school's own record of detentions and complaints sits where it sat a decade earlier. The judgement is about a generation, and no pupil any of them can name is offered as the evidence for it.

examples.tag: The trade that is not what it was
examples.text: A plumber says customers no longer settle up and tradesmen no longer do honest work, though his books show the same share of late payers as when he started. Decline is asserted about the trade in general while the records of it stay flat.

replication.headline: An independent group repeated study 5b with 533 participants in 2024 and all four of its primary findings held.
replication.detail: Transparent Replications by Clearer Thinking ran study 5b again with 533 participants after exclusions, drawn from 721 who took the survey, aged 18 to 69 and stratified across ten age groups. Perceived decline from twenty years after the participant's birth to the present day held, t = -13.915, P < 0.001, as did decline from the birth year to twenty years later, t = -6.015, P < 0.001. Neither comparison covering years before the participant was born showed a difference, and equivalence tests accepted both, P = 0.003 and P = 0.034. The original had accepted equivalence on only one of those two, so the replication came out slightly cleaner than the paper it tested. The report gave the original paper five stars for replicability and 4.25 for transparency, marking it down because study 5b was not preregistered. Mastroianni and Gilbert also report two direct repeats of their own study 2a, one of them preregistered, with the same results. What has been repeated is the perception, not the archival argument. No independent redoing of study 4, the analysis that carries the claim that nothing has actually declined, was located.

study.cite: Transparent Replications by Clearer Thinking (2024). Report #10: Replication of a study from "The illusion of moral decline" (Nature | Mastroianni & Gilbert 2023).

limits: The strong claim is that morality has not declined, and the evidence for it is subjective. Mastroianni and Gilbert say so themselves, writing that their measures "are not definitive" while arguing that the wording of items about queues and strangers is too concrete to have drifted in meaning. The one objective figure they offer, a rise in prisoner's dilemma cooperation between 1956 and 2017, is credited to Yuan and colleagues and is quoted here from their description of it rather than from that paper. Their original studies used only US samples, and the non-US archival items span 13 years, from 1996 to 2007, against 70 for the US series. Decline is not the default belief about everything. Hillman, Antoun and Hauser report five studies of an improvement default, in which people presume things have got better in domains they know nothing about, including historical periods that in fact declined. Beliefs about the young are also domain-specific rather than global. Protzko and Schooler found that the average American did not think children were less intelligent than in the past, P > 0.81, though that sample was small, at 134, beside the 1,824 and 1,500 of the other two trait studies. Study 5a rests on its exclusions, and Mastroianni and Gilbert say so: with the excluded participants restored, the overall perception of decline and the personal-change effect stop being significant. No peer-reviewed rebuttal of the 2023 paper was found on 21 September 2026. OpenAlex then recorded 52 citing works, Europe PMC listed 14 and returned no comment or letter to a title search, and the article page at nature.com carries no Matters Arising. The critiques located were blog posts and are not cited here.
misreadings: Declinism is not rosy retrospection, entry 81, and the two are routinely merged. Rosy retrospection compares one person's later rating of an event against the rating they gave while it was happening. Declinism is a judgement about other people across historical time. They come apart in the data. In Mastroianni and Gilbert's study 5a the same respondents said people in general had got worse while the people they personally knew had got better. The second error is a unit error. The figure 84.18% is the share of survey items on which a majority reported decline, not the share of people who believe in decline. The third is treating it as a political marking. More conservative respondents perceived more decline, but liberal respondents perceived decline too, M = -0.35, t(398) = -4.96, P < 0.001, d = 0.28 in study 2a. Protzko and Schooler found political conservatism unrelated to the belief that children no longer enjoy reading, P > 0.25. Older people are not more prone to it in the way the stereotype suggests. Older respondents reported more total decline, and study 2c showed this was because they were reporting across more years: the perceived annual rate did not differ by age, b = -0.0002, 95% CI [-0.0005, 0.0002], P = 0.29. The last error is reading the illusion as settled for every domain. It is a claim about aggregate perception across survey items, and where objective series exist, as with recorded crime, the mismatch has to be shown against those series rather than assumed.

In Social and Psychological Bases of Ideology and System Justification, 402-424. Oxford University Press. Cited for the existence of the argument linking perceived decline to conservative politics, which the chapter's own abstract and opening pages carry. Read as a scan of pages 402 to 417, taken from an archived copy of the authors' laboratory page; the closing pages were not in that file.
